short: Three centuries usually taken as imperial China's cosmopolitan high point.
full:
Li Yuan took the throne in 618 and was displaced within eight years by his son Li Shimin, who killed two brothers at the Xuanwu Gate and ruled as Taizong. Under him and his successors the Tang pushed garrisons deep into Central Asia, and Chang'an grew into a walled grid city of perhaps a million people, with Sogdian merchants, Persian refugees, Nestorian churches and a Japanese embassy quarter. Officials were increasingly recruited through the examination system, and the empire ran on the equal-field allotment of land and militia service.

The An Lushan rebellion of 755 broke that settlement permanently. Afterwards the court survived by conceding autonomy to regional military governors and by taxing the salt trade, and its authority never recovered. Cultural output did not decline with it: Li Bai and Du Fu wrote during the wars, woodblock printing spread, and the world's earliest dated printed book was produced in 868. Huang Chao's rebels sacked both capitals in the 880s, and in 907 the warlord Zhu Wen deposed the last emperor.
